summary: Describes benefits of applications using transports with Explicit Congestion Notification, such as throughput and delay gains when routers mark packets, and challenges to deployment.

eli5.summary: Routers can whisper that traffic is getting heavy instead of dropping messages. This explains why that is nicer.

subtitle: How routers can signal congestion early without dropping packets.

tldr.problem: Networks need to signal congestion to applications, but packet loss is an inefficient and disruptive way to do it.
tldr.mechanism: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets routers mark packets with a congestion signal instead of dropping them, giving endpoints advance warning of network congestion.
tldr.outcome: Applications using ECN-capable transports experience better throughput, lower latency, and faster congestion detection across network paths where routers support ECN.

today: RFC 8087 is an Informational RFC describing the benefits and requirements for ECN deployment. It has not been obsoleted. Network support for ECN has grown since publication, but ECN remains an optional feature that endpoints must negotiate.

sections.title: What is ECN
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) is a way for network devices to signal that the network is becoming congested. Instead of dropping packets when queues fill up—which requires the application to detect loss and retransmit—ECN marks the packet with a congestion flag that the receiving application can see and report back.

ECN is carried in a 2-bit field in the IP header of every IPv4 and IPv6 packet. This field has four possible values: Not-ECT (meaning the packet does not use ECN), two ECT values indicating the endpoint supports ECN, and CE (Congestion Experienced) which a router sets to signal congestion. When a router marks a packet with CE, it is telling the receiving endpoint 'I see congestion ahead; ask your sender to slow down.'
sections.eli5: Every packet has a 2-bit label. Routers can flip one bit to say 'it's getting crowded.' The endpoint sees this and tells the sender.

sections.title: Key Benefits of Using ECN
sections.content:
ECN provides several important benefits when enabled end-to-end across a congested path. First, it improves throughput by eliminating the wasteful need to retransmit packets that already traversed most of the network successfully; a packet marked with CE still arrives intact at its destination, whereas a dropped packet must be sent again from scratch. Second, it reduces latency for applications that require in-order delivery. When a packet is lost, the receiving end must wait for retransmission before passing any later data to the application (a delay called head-of-line blocking). ECN eliminates this delay by delivering the marked packet immediately.

A third benefit is reducing the probability of Retransmission Timeout (RTO) expiry, which causes a large, sudden reduction in sending rate. ECN marks packets early, before the sender times out waiting for lost packets. Fourth, latency-critical applications like voice and video do not retransmit lost packets anyway; they can only adjust their sending rate. ECN lets these applications react to incipient congestion before loss occurs, avoiding the need for recovery techniques like forward error correction that consume extra bandwidth. Finally, ECN makes the presence of congestion visible and measurable, which can inform network operations and enable new, more responsive congestion control algorithms.
sections.eli5: Marked packets arrive faster than dropped ones because they don't need retransmission. Voice calls detect congestion early and don't need to hide dropped data. Operators can see how much congestion is happening.

sections.title: Network Requirements for ECN
sections.content:
For ECN to work, the entire network path must properly handle ECN-capable packets. At minimum, every router along the path must forward packets that carry ECN codepoints (the ECT values), even if the router itself does not perform ECN marking. Routers that incorrectly drop ECN-capable packets prevent the endpoint from seeing any benefit.

Routers that do support ECN should use Active Queue Management (AQM) to set the CE mark on packets when the router detects incipient congestion. The key design rule is: a router should CE-mark a packet at the point where it would otherwise have dropped it, signaling the beginning of congestion before the queue overflows. A critical requirement is that no router must 'bleach' (reset) a CE-marked packet back to a non-ECN value, because that hides the congestion signal from the receiver. If a router cannot forward a CE-marked packet, it must drop the packet entirely rather than bleach the marking.
sections.eli5: Routers need to know about the 2-bit label and not ignore it. The best ones mark packets early. Nobody is allowed to erase a congestion mark once it is set.

sections.title: Partial Deployment and Fallback
sections.content:
ECN is designed for incremental deployment. Endpoints negotiate ECN support before using it, so a sender can enable ECN only when both endpoints agree and the application requires it. This means ECN-capable endpoints can coexist with regular endpoints on the same network without conflict.

However, the Internet has historically suffered from middleboxes and misconfigured routers that bleach or drop ECN-capable packets. To remain robust, endpoints must detect when the network path does not properly support ECN and fall back to loss-based congestion control. A sender can verify ECN support by intentionally marking certain test packets with CE and observing whether the receiver correctly reports them. If a sender detects that CE marks are not reaching the receiver, or that the receiver is not reporting them (cheating), the sender should disable ECN for that flow and rely solely on loss detection. This approach lets ECN deployment proceed gradually while applications continue to work correctly across non-supporting networks.
sections.eli5: Not every network supports ECN yet. Endpoints can ask 'does this path support ECN?' and switch to the old method if the answer is no.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: This document introduces no new security considerations beyond those discussed in the referenced RFCs that define ECN itself and transport protocols. Designers implementing ECN should be aware that a receiver could falsely report that it received CE marks it did not actually see, and senders should include mechanisms to detect this kind of misbehavior. Similarly, a network device could mark packets incorrectly or bleach valid marks, which is why endpoints need to detect and fall back from broken ECN paths.
sections.eli5: Receivers could lie about seeing congestion marks. Senders should check that the receivers are honest.
